claims.text: Brief line 1 title: form a platform team before the second product team; lines 3-7: asks leadership to agree; effect: new shops open sooner (product teams stop building/keeping cluster, deploy, monitoring), shops keep SLOs in docs/design/slo.md; all numbers are assumptions.

Brief lines 11-15: A do nothing (keep 7-person team; no new people; new shops, managed Kubernetes, prod monitoring queue in one team; cluster one person); B grow to 14 (7 people, 2-3 sprints; pairs 21->91); C platform 3-4 first, then Cửa hàng 5-7 (one person for 2 sprints; second team starts later).
Brief lines 17-18: with C, the Cửa hàng team deploys through the path the platform team already keeps, without learning the cluster from scratch.

Brief lines 20-24: the platform team needs 3 to 4 people, the right number depends on the move of production to managed Kubernetes, not yet estimated; taking over the shared parts (the cluster, deploy, monitoring of lines 4-5) takes 2 to 3 sprints.

Brief lines 26-33, change signals: requests to the platform team often answered after > 2 working days = platform short of people; shops growing slower than multi-shop-requirements.md = delay Cửa hàng team; two teams changing one part in most changes = boundary wrong.

Brief lines 35-47: if no, keep A, do the 'Next' outcomes of roadmap.md (middle of three horizons: now, next, later) one at a time, report the order so leadership picks the first (37-39); effect visible when Cửa hàng ships to production with nobody outside helping deploy (46-47).
Brief lines 49-55, appendix: ADR 0025 for the decision and options weighed; team-structure.md for today's team, ownership and how teams work together; roadmap.md for outcomes waiting for people.

ADR 0025 is accepted; lines 26-49 weigh a bigger team, layer teams, and stream-aligned teams with a platform team; lines 57-59 reject layer teams because nearly every change a shop can see needs all three teams.
Leaders weigh many requests with little time for each, so a brief opens with the ask, the recommendation and its business effect; a leader who stops after that paragraph still knows what to decide.

Including doing nothing among the options (leaders can usually choose it, and it has a cost), each with cost in people and sprints and what it gives up, lets leaders choose instead of only approving or refusing the single choice shown.
A confident number that later moves usually costs more trust than a range given up front; a change signal named in advance lets a later change read as an expected step.

Technical reasoning is not deleted but kept in the documents that already hold it, linked from the appendix; likely hard questions, starting with 'what if no?', get prepared answers, so a refusal still ends the meeting with a decision.

Trade-offs: background first fits when readers are the deciding team; recommendation only fits small reversible decisions; ask first with options fits decisions costing people or sprints; one number fits measured values; range plus signals fits unestimated ones.

Choices: asked for one number, give the range with its reason and offer the upper end to plan with; an engineering leader wanting detail is walked through the appendix; a refusal still ends with a decision via lines 37-39.
Symptoms (hedged): a meeting ends with 'send us something shorter' and the decision moves; a leader asks what else was considered; a promised number moves and the next request meets more doubt.

beyond_scope: Section 5 compares the brief option set with ADR 0025 (lines 26-49) to show which reasoning stays in the appendix.
